decision: Alonso's 1-for-6 start is noise, but his recent-seasons prior gives about a 60% chance he never gets above .250 this year.
original_tool: Bayesian Beta-Binomial
anova_analysis: none possible (one player, no groups)
why: The decision is the probability of one player's future season, which a t-test cannot express.

decision: The Jets' first-round hit rate (5 of 17) is worse than chance would usually give a league-average drafter, and they miss most on the high picks.
original_tool: simulation of hit counts against league rate
anova_analysis: one-sample/two-sample t-test of Jets pick hit (0/1) vs league picks
why: With 17 binary picks the t-test gives p near .07, so the analyst would call the Jets no different from average where the issue says they underperform.

decision: Soto's calf has about a 54% chance of costing him 10+ games, and his absence costs the Mets a real share of their offense.
original_tool: Bayesian injury-duration model
anova_analysis: none possible (single future injury)
why: The chance of one player missing 10 games is a single-event probability the tool cannot pose.

decision: Basketball is the sport where losing one star sinks a team; baseball almost never, because of how many players share the field and the minutes.
original_tool: Beta-Binomial posterior simulation of with/without-star seasons, one case per sport
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of game win (0/1) with vs without the star, separately for each sport's case
why: The t-tests would find huge effects for the LeBron, Manning and Price cases and a non-significant 95-67 vs 85-77 for baseball, read as 'no effect', where the issue says 10 wins with an interval crossing zero.

decision: The Mets' .500 record is an offense problem; the pitching is good.
original_tool: descriptive comparisons of team pitching and hitting lines
anova_analysis: t-tests of Mets runs allowed and runs scored per game against league averages
why: Simple comparisons of runs allowed vs scored against league would point to the offense the same way the issue does.

decision: Two AP rankings closer than about 13 spots are not reliably distinguishable; arguments over #8 vs #11 are noise.
original_tool: win-rate by rank gap against a 75% JND threshold
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA (or t-tests) of higher-ranked-team win (0/1) across rank-gap bins, n=1,597
why: With 1,597 games even small rank gaps beat 50% significantly, so the analyst would declare every rank difference real, the opposite of the JND conclusion.

decision: A rate stat means little until it reaches its stabilization threshold (e.g., about 910 AB for batting average, 60 PA for strikeout rate); trust career rates before then.
original_tool: published reliability/stabilization thresholds
anova_analysis: none possible (the tool assumes stats are measured without error)
why: How many trials a stat needs before it is reliable is a measurement question the error-free one-tool analyst never asks.

decision: Mason Miller is spectacular, but 6 1/3 innings is far too small a sample to call him the most unhittable pitcher ever.
original_tool: small-sample reasoning, role comparison and a cohort of past hot relievers
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of Miller's opponent hits per batter faced vs Pedro Martinez 2000 or league pitchers
why: Over 34 innings his .063 vs Pedro's .167 would test significant, and the analyst would call him more unhittable, ignoring the closer-vs-starter ruler and stabilization the issue rests on.

decision: An owner index z-scored within league ranks owners differently from championship counts; the top and bottom are not who the headlines say.
original_tool: composite of three z-scored metrics within league
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of team win% by owner (no way to build a ranking)
why: The decision is a cross-league ranking on standardized rulers, which the tool cannot produce.

decision: The Mets-Braves rivalry is lopsided: 17 division titles to 2 since 1995 and a 510-419 head-to-head.
original_tool: descriptive counts
anova_analysis: none needed (descriptive record)
why: A historical tally involves no inference to get wrong.

decision: Team patience barely tracks wins because teams differ so little in pitches per PA; the eye is half-right, not wrong.
original_tool: correlation with range-restriction explanation
anova_analysis: median split of 30 teams on P/PA, two-sample t-test of wins
why: The t-test would come out non-significant and be read as 'patience does nothing', missing the range-restriction point that the issue makes.

decision: Carolina's 8-0 start is the first sweep of the first two rounds in the four-round best-of-seven era.
original_tool: descriptive historical record
anova_analysis: none needed (descriptive record)
why: A record-book fact involves no inference to get wrong.

decision: BaseRuns, built from the Mets' hits, walks and total bases, tells you whether their runs and record match their underlying play.
original_tool: BaseRuns run estimator vs Pythagorean
anova_analysis: none possible (no expected-runs model)
why: The analyst takes runs scored as measured without error, which is exactly the assumption BaseRuns exists to question.

decision: Superstitions look like they work because a ritual started during a slump is followed by the regression that was coming anyway.
original_tool: regression-to-the-mean argument
anova_analysis: paired t-test of performance before vs after the ritual
why: A before-after paired t-test after a slump would come out significant and 'prove' the ritual works.

decision: The Astros' tank worked for Houston but taxed the league as a commons, which is why MLB added a draft lottery.
original_tool: historical narrative and incentive argument
anova_analysis: t-test of later win% for tanking vs non-tanking clubs
why: The issue is a historical and incentive argument (274 losses, three No. 1 picks) with no inference for the tool to get wrong.

decision: At the top, roster spending is so compressed that the marginal dollar buys a seat among contenders, not the title; the 2026 spending responded to 2025, not the reverse.
original_tool: arithmetic on published valuations plus cited research
anova_analysis: t-test of win% or titles for the six $40M+ rosters vs the next tier
why: A non-significant gap inside the top tier would be read as 'money does nothing at the top', near the issue's point but stated as absence, and the tool never asks the causal direction the issue corrected.

decision: Notre Dame drew outsized outrage for spending less than Texas because coverage tracks violated expectations, not dollars.
original_tool: descriptive comparison and expectation-violation argument
anova_analysis: none possible (no outcome measured)
why: The coverage asymmetry is argued, not measured, so there is no analysis the tool could change.

decision: Most first basemen's careers end early (half gone by year five); the aging curve describes only the survivors.
original_tool: survival / half-life on every debut
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of performance by career year among active players
why: An ANOVA over players still active would draw the survivor-only aging curve the issue was written to debunk.

decision: Matched at equal scales, baseball's year-over-year predictability still beats snowfall in both fair comparisons.
original_tool: Pearson correlations at matched aggregation scales
anova_analysis: median split prior-year value, t-test this-year value, separately for baseball and snow
why: Baseball would still come out significant and snow not, but pooled team-years would be treated as independent and the scale issue never raised.

decision: Two champions finishing 16-3 a day apart is less surprising than it looks once you count the base rate of 16-3 runs.
original_tool: base-rate probability
anova_analysis: none possible (chance of a coincidence)
why: The decision is the probability of a coincidence, which the tool has no way to express.

decision: Notre Dame clears the blue-chip floor with 17 other teams and has matched Alabama's recruiting, but not its development (16 vs 2 first-round picks) or consistency; a contender, not a dynasty.
original_tool: necessary-vs-sufficient reasoning; recruiting ranks vs NFL draft output
anova_analysis: t-test of blue-chip ratio, champions vs non-champions; t-test of recruiting rank, ND vs Alabama
why: The analyst would read a significant champion gap as 'high blue-chip wins titles' and a non-significant ND-Alabama recruiting gap as 'peers', missing that inputs and developed output are different rulers.

decision: Indiana won with an 8% blue-chip ratio; the 20-year rule was a summary of conditions that changed, not a law.
original_tool: descriptive history plus regime-change argument
anova_analysis: t-test of blue-chip ratio for champions vs others, Indiana included
why: With one new case the champion-vs-rest gap stays significant, so the analyst keeps the 'law' the issue says broke.

decision: Valenzuela's five straight All-Star strikeouts in 1986 matched Hubbell's 1934 feat and has not been done since.
original_tool: descriptive historical record
anova_analysis: none needed (descriptive record)
why: A record-book fact involves no inference to get wrong.

decision: Once the three-point line is included, Clark's statistical twin is no longer Oscar Robertson; the match depends on which dimensions you count.
original_tool: distance matching on team-share stat profiles
anova_analysis: none possible (no similarity measure)
why: Finding a player's nearest match across eras is outside anything a t-test can pose.

decision: Payroll and winning are related but weakly; money explains about 15% of wins.
original_tool: correlation over 2022-25 payrolls
anova_analysis: median split payroll, two-sample t-test of wins over team-seasons
why: A significant high-vs-low payroll t-test reads as 'money buys wins', losing the 15%-of-variance size (the codebook's own example).

decision: A four-year average lags; a program's slope and the bend in its slope show where it is heading (Indiana is still .500 on its average).
original_tool: rolling slope and curvature of win%
anova_analysis: paired t-test of recent seasons vs earlier block for each program
why: Collapsing seasons into before/after blocks gives the rearview-mirror average the issue argues against, so movers are caught late.

decision: Down one late, pulling the goalie lowers your expected margin but raises your chance to win from about 3% to 5%, so you do it.
original_tool: win-probability model
anova_analysis: t-test of goal differential with goalie pulled vs in net
why: The t-test shows a significantly worse goal margin with the net empty and would advise never pulling, flipping the decision.

decision: A team that wins 29 of 100 over a season wins about 48 of 100 in one sudden-death game, which is why upsets feel so sweet.
original_tool: probability arithmetic for single games
anova_analysis: none possible (single-game win probability)
why: The decision is a single-game probability, which the tool cannot express.

decision: Ohio State football made $33M while the athletic department lost $38M; which number you get depends on where you draw the box.
original_tool: accounting at two levels
anova_analysis: none needed (budget arithmetic)
why: Budget arithmetic involves no inference to get wrong.

decision: Skenes is not declining: his strikeouts, walks and homers are as before; ERA and record reflect his defense and run support.
original_tool: decomposition into fielding-independent components
anova_analysis: t-test of Skenes's per-start ERA this season vs last
why: Treating ERA as a clean measure of the pitcher, a significant gap would read as decline, the reverse of the issue's answer.

decision: Boston's 25-3 run is real but roughly one-in-70,000 luck; 1 of 109 comparable teams made it, so it teaches nothing general.
original_tool: base rates over 109 comparable clubs and run probability
anova_analysis: paired t-test of Boston's win rate before vs after July 3
why: A significant before-after jump would be read as a real change (belief rewarded), the lesson the issue warns against.

decision: Notre Dame keeps about 27% of its in-season attention in the dead months, but so does everyone; it ranks 7th of 12.
original_tool: ratios of median monthly pageviews, correlation with CI
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of off-season attention share across 12 programs (months as rows)
why: The ANOVA would find Notre Dame unremarkable among the blue bloods, the same answer.

decision: Only one Mets series, four games against Philadelphia, really matters, because most remaining opponents are not teams they must pass.
original_tool: playoff-leverage simulation
anova_analysis: none possible (leverage of future games)
why: Ranking future games by how much playoff probability they move is a forecast the tool cannot make.

decision: Boston is the better club but six games back is a fact while superiority is a rate, so Tampa Bay will likely win the division anyway.
original_tool: run differential rate and deficit-clearing arithmetic / odds
anova_analysis: t-test of per-game run differential, Boston vs Tampa Bay
why: The tool can compare teams but cannot say who will win the division, which is the decision.

decision: An opening-week win is worth about 1.5 extra wins after controlling for talent; one game says more than the summer's indicators.
original_tool: OLS with talent and returning-production controls, R-squared change
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of final win% for week-one winners vs losers
why: The naive t-test also says the opener matters (1.8 wins) but folds talent into the gap the issue controls for.

decision: We could not find that Cleveland ruins careers; joiners there were more likely to keep playing (9th of 32), so our earlier claim was wrong.
original_tool: logistic regression with experience and snap-share controls; club effects
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of two-year survival (0/1) across 32 clubs
why: A non-significant club ANOVA would also clear Cleveland, but by reading a null on an uncontrolled binary outcome as proof of no effect.

decision: Detroit's +55 run differential says about 79 wins; the 12-games-under record sits in one-run games, which is mostly luck.
original_tool: Pythagorean expectation plus a year-over-year persistence correlation for one-run records
anova_analysis: median split clubs on one-run win%, t-test next season's one-run win%
why: The t-test would come out non-significant and say one-run records do not repeat, but as proof of absence and with no expected-wins figure, which the issue backs with a control correlation.

decision: The NFL home edge vanished in 2019 with full crowds, so empty 2020 stadiums were not the test they seemed; crowds probably are not the cause.
original_tool: season margins with 95% intervals and two-sample t-tests
anova_analysis: two-sample t-tests of home margin, 2016-18 vs 2019 vs 2020
why: The issue itself used these t-tests, so the one-tool analyst gets the same answer for the same reason.

decision: Of a dozen booth stats only four predict later wins once you hold the score fixed; the rest just restate the score.
original_tool: partial correlations controlling for point margin
anova_analysis: median split each stat, t-test later win rate (n=320 team-seasons)
why: Without controlling for score, every stat's split would be significant, so the analyst would call all twelve useful.

decision: Houston and Texas are tied at 79-80; there is about a 70% chance the AL West winner finishes with the first losing record among 270 division winners.
original_tool: simulation of remaining games plus historical counts
anova_analysis: none possible (probability of a future record)
why: The 70% chance is a single-event forecast the tool cannot express.

decision: Susana's line reads three levels but the transaction log shows one real promotion; misclassification decides the answer before any arithmetic.
original_tool: record checking / classification of transactions
anova_analysis: t-test of later outcomes for 'fast-promoted' vs other prospects using season-line levels
why: Taking the season line at face value, the analyst would count three promotions and put the wrong players in the sample.

decision: A new coach's roster is all inherited at first and fully his only by year five; year-one jumps are often regression, and firing a middling coach tends to make things worse.
original_tool: roster-share counting curve plus cited research
anova_analysis: paired t-test of team record before vs after a coaching change
why: Coaches are fired at a low point, so a before-after t-test would credit the new coach with the rebound.

decision: Ohtani's 3-for-24 is what chance looks like; a coin hitter with his talent goes that cold about four times a year, the real Ohtani about once.
original_tool: simulation of streaks under a binomial null
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of Ohtani's playoff vs season hit rate (at-bats as 0/1)
why: A non-significant test would also call it noise, but only by reading a null as absence, and it cannot show he slumps less than chance.

decision: Bad teams improve about 3 points a year whether or not they change coaches; Indiana's 2024 +28 was a one-time outlier.
original_tool: comparison of changers vs keepers on SP+ change
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of next-year SP+ change, bad teams that changed coaches vs kept them
why: The issue's core comparison is a two-group difference that a t-test reproduces, with keepers as the control.

decision: Coaches who return to their alma mater win no more (47% vs 46%); what differs is the program they were handed.
original_tool: comparison of win% with adjustment for prior five-year record
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of win% for alumni vs other coaches
why: The t-test also finds no edge but reads p>.05 as proof, and misses the adjusted gap with an interval and the inherited-program story.

decision: A quarterback's record largely reflects his defense: teams win 86% when allowing under 17 and 16% when allowing 28+.
original_tool: win rates by points-allowed bins
anova_analysis: one-way ANOVA of win (0/1) across points-allowed groups
why: With 13,934 starts the grouped comparison gives the same overwhelming gap the issue reports.

decision: A cap fight has stopped games 10 of 12 times; a lockout is about 5 in 6 and lost games next spring about 1 in 3.
original_tool: historical base rates
anova_analysis: none possible (probability of a future lockout)
why: The decision is the chance of one future event, which the tool cannot express.

decision: Losing assistants does not sink a head coach; the next-year slide is regression after a big season, and raided teams outperform matched teams over three years.
original_tool: regression model controlling for this season and prior average
anova_analysis: paired t-test of win% the season before vs after an assistant leaves
why: The before-after drop is significant and would be read as 'propped up by his staff', the reverse of the issue's finding.

decision: Of 15 first-half worries, 7 held, 4 were noise; worries about team records held, worries about one player's first week mostly did not.
original_tool: grading tally of past claims against final numbers
anova_analysis: none needed (counting graded claims)
why: Grading past claims is a tally with no inference for the tool to get wrong.

decision: Georgia is the likeliest champion at about 28 in 100 (plausibly 6 to 60), and below it the field is close to coin flips.
original_tool: season and bracket simulation with rating uncertainty
anova_analysis: none possible (title probabilities)
why: Championship probabilities are forecasts the tool cannot produce.

decision: NHL goals per team-game follow a Poisson distribution from the average alone (about 5-6 shutouts per 100); the misses show score effects.
original_tool: Poisson model fit to 27,000 team-games
anova_analysis: none possible (t-test treats goals as normal; no distribution fit)
why: The analyst treats goals as normal and has no way to predict how often 0, 1 or 7 goals occur.

decision: The executive order's transfer limits, NIL caps and eligibility rules will push blue-blood title share back toward 78-83%.
original_tool: descriptive title shares by era plus judgment projection
anova_analysis: two-sample t-test of blue-blood title (0/1), pre-portal vs portal era
why: The decision is a projected future title share under the order, which the tool cannot make; a 12-title portal-era comparison would also come out non-significant and be read as no change.
